solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old money duke occasionally unchaste

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for duke

indicators.note: something done only occasionally happens at intervals, so only every other letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: An aristocrat of old whose wealth came with a loose reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: A ducat was a gold or silver coin once used across Europe, so it is a historical currency.

clue.text: Funny joke drolly entertaining court physician

indicators.note: funny here means odd or peculiar, so the letters that follow are put into a strange new order
to entertain a guest is to take them in, so the jumbled letters hold another piece inside

parts.note: the ten letters of both words, rearranged
CT is the usual abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A doctor who amuses the court with dry wit, like a royal jester.
explanation.walkthrough: CT goes in after the first two letters of the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's Dr Jekyll is a fictional medical man who turns into Mr Hyde, so he is an example of a physician.

clue.text: Cut meat desire following slight stomach upset

indicators.note: a slight upset in the stomach means only the middle of the word is disturbed, just two neighbouring letters swapping places

parts.note: to crave is to desire strongly

explanation.surface: A craving for meat that comes on after a bout of indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second and third letters change places, a 'slight' disturbance in the middle of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To carve is to slice a joint of meat for serving, a verb matching the imperative-looking definition.

clue.text: Came together and did rock record for Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words here trade places

parts.note: to rock something is to shake it; past tense
to tape is to record
say the two words with their opening sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A band that played rock music and made a recording together.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds SH and T of the two words to get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plan takes shape its parts come together into a definite form, an idiom for coalescing.

clue.text: Sumptuous taste, mostly ace £1 sandwiches

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to place it between two layers, so the number is held inside the other letters
mostly means most but not all of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a palate is a sense of taste
A is the card abbreviation for ace
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pound
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone with refined taste lavishing money on an ace, as in a luxury lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: PALAT plus A and L forms a casing around I, which sits between the T and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Palatial describes something as grand and luxurious as a palace, a close synonym of sumptuous.

clue.text: Dad's traversing peak of Moroccan plains

indicators.note: to traverse is to go across, so the father's word stretches across and around the letter that follows

parts.note: papa is dad; plural reading of the possessive

indicators.note: the peak is the top, which in a down answer is the opening letter of the word

parts.note: the first letter

explanation.surface: Father crossing the summit of a mountain in Morocco.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's is read as 'papas' (Dad's = dads), and M is placed after the opening PA.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are the vast grassy lowlands of Argentina and Uruguay, so they are plains.

clue.text: Hang around wearing underwear that is stolen

indicators.note: if something is stolen it is taken away, so those letters are removed from the garment word

parts.note: lingerie is women's underwear
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'
clothes being worn are on

explanation.surface: A thief wearing the underwear he has stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: To linger on is to stay longer than expected, a phrasal verb meaning to hang around.

clue.text: Penniless subject admitting vote is harmful

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so the shortened word takes a letter inside
penniless means without a penny, and a penny is abbreviated P, so that letter goes

parts.note: a topic is a subject of discussion
a cross marks a vote on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A broke citizen's vote does harm to the state.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the abbreviation for penny, the coin a penniless person lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Toxic means poisonous, and by extension anything that causes damage or harm.

clue.text: Coming inside undressed, sailor boy turned up — such muscle!

definitions.note: the definition is adjectival: describing a muscle of this kind

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

indicators.note: inside tells us the stripped word goes within another piece
in a down answer turning a word up makes it read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of its outer covering, so the first and last letters are taken off

parts.note: the word without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A naked sailor boy turns up indoors, showing off his physique.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'turned up' reads naturally as reversal; the stripped word then sits inside the reversed boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Abdominal muscles are the 'abs' of the belly, so the adjective describes that kind of muscle.

clue.text: Zany Bronx comedian receives Oscar for harmful, tasteless stuff

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so the scrambled letters hold another inside
zany means crazy and erratic, so these letters are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: the fodder letters
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A crazy New York comic wins an Oscar for a tasteless, harmful act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tasteless' looks like a jibe at the comedian's humour; it is literal, describing a gas with no flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no colour, smell or flavour, hence harmful and tasteless.

clue.text: Holy Thursday always involves dissonance, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests something gone wrong or badly, so the letters are disordered
to involve is to wrap up or include, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: ay (aye) is an old word for always
its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A lament that this sacred day always brings musical discord.
explanation.walkthrough: Ay, meaning ever or always, survives in poetry and Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascension Day, forty days after Easter, always falls on a Thursday, and is also called Holy Thursday.

clue.text: Exaggerate the introduction of obscure poetry full of rubbish

indicators.note: an introduction comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: its first letter

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so the poetry word wraps around the rubbish word

parts.note: verse is poetry
tat is cheap, worthless stuff

explanation.surface: A critic overstating how obscure and rubbishy some poetry is.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstate is to say more than the facts warrant, a direct synonym of exaggerate.

clue.text: Academic stream pursued by American novelist and essayist

parts.note: the Cam is the river flowing through Cambridge, a university town
US is short for American

explanation.surface: A university river followed along by an American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pursued by' puts the American piece after the stream.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus, the French author of The Outsider and The Myth of Sisyphus, wrote both novels and essays.

clue.text: Man left holding a dog

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within your grasp, so the word for a man plus left wraps around the article

parts.note: jack is a generic word for a man, as in every man jack
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A man who has gone off leaving someone to look after his dog.
explanation.walkthrough: JACK and L together hold A between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackal is a wild member of the dog family found in Africa and Asia.

clue.text: Dreary toast the French consumed

indicators.note: something consumed is taken in, so the toast word swallows the French article

parts.note: cheers is said when raising a toast
les is French for 'the' (plural)

explanation.surface: A dismal toast given while the French ate their meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerless describes something gloomy and lacking any brightness, which is what dreary means.

clue.text: Famous statue put back outside former capital city university

indicators.note: outside means the reversed word goes around the city
put back means returned the way it came, so the statue's name is read backwards

parts.note: the statue of Eros stands in London's Piccadilly Circus
Bonn was the capital of West Germany

explanation.surface: A well-known statue returned to the grounds of a university in a former capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The Piccadilly Circus statue, popularly called Eros, is a London landmark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sorbonne is the historic university in Paris, so it is a university by name.

clue.text: A serial wife-killer, depressed poet swallows drug

parts.note: feeling blue is feeling depressed

indicators.note: to swallow is to take in, so the poet word encloses the drug

parts.note: a bard is a poet
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A gloomy poet who kills his wives, swallowing pills.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluebeard is the folk-tale nobleman who murdered a succession of wives, an archetypal serial killer.

clue.text: Terribly sore knee that might become inflamed

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: something that might catch fire

indicators.note: terribly suggests badly out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A painful knee joint that could swell up and become inflamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflamed' reads as medical swelling, but here it means set on fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Kerosene is paraffin, a fuel oil that can be set alight, so it might become inflamed in the literal sense.

clue.text: Crucial newspaper boss acquiring Evening Observer so described?

definitions.note: the definition describes an observer; the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: acquiring means taking on, so the crucial word takes the evening word inside

parts.note: key means crucial
e'en is the poetic contraction of evening
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: An important editor takes on the Evening Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday paper, which makes it look like a title; here it means a watcher. E'EN goes after the K.
explanation.definitionFit: A good observer has sharp sight, so keen-eyed describes such a person.

clue.text: Doubts question put to charity

parts.note: QU is an abbreviation for question
alms are charitable gifts

explanation.surface: Someone raising doubts and questioning a charity.
explanation.definitionFit: Qualms are uneasy misgivings, a plural noun matching doubts.

clue.text: Upper-class fur available for exploitation

parts.note: U stands for upper-class
sable is a costly fur

explanation.surface: Posh people's furs being exploited for profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something usable can be put to use, so it is available to be exploited.

clue.text: Playing slowly a necessity for popular golfer

indicators.note: something that is a necessity for a phrase is an essential part of it, so the answer is found within the words

parts.note: inside, across the word break

explanation.surface: A well-liked golfer needs to play at a slow pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing slowly' looks like slow play on the golf course; it is the musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is a tempo marking telling musicians to perform slowly and broadly.

clue.text: G8 say or voice Tweets every now and again

indicators.note: now and again means at regular intervals, so only every second letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: World leaders at a summit speaking their minds on social media posts.
explanation.walkthrough: The G8 was a forum of eight leading nations, so it is an example of a group of eight.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is any set of eight, and the G8 was a group of eight countries.

clue.text: Old firm fed retired copper — top man! — Italian food

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: O is short for old

indicators.note: something fed has food put into it, so the old firm letters take the other pieces inside

parts.note: Co is short for company
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
the boss is the top man

explanation.surface: A long-established company feeding its retired policeman, the old boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal, and 'retired' acts on both the metal and the top man together.
explanation.definitionFit: Osso bucco is a Milanese dish of braised veal shanks, so it is Italian food.

clue.text: Line dance?

parts.note: surface reading: country-and-western line dancing, with dancers in rows
setter's reading: a Latin party dance done in a single snaking queue, each dancer holding the one in front

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'line dance' is meant literally, a dance in one line, not the cowboy style.
explanation.definitionFit: This Cuban dance is performed by people in a single file, hip to hip, so it is literally danced in a line.

clue.text: Empty-headed eejit initially punches dad, hit on the noggin

indicators.note: a punch lands inside someone's guard, so the letter goes into the parent word

parts.note: dad is father

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of the Irish insult is used

parts.note: first letter; eejit is Irish slang for idiot
to brain someone is to strike them on the head; noggin is slang for head

explanation.surface: A foolish lad hits his father on the head in a family brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes after the F.
explanation.definitionFit: Feather-brained means silly, as if the head held nothing weightier than feathers, so empty-headed.

clue.text: Sweatier when running, so to speak

indicators.note: running suggests letters on the move, so they shift into a different order

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A jogger gets sweatier while out on a run, figuratively speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: As it were and so to speak are both phrases used to flag an expression as figurative.

clue.text: Current article features in humourless journal

indicators.note: to feature in something is to appear within it, so the first pieces sit inside the humourless word

parts.note: dry can mean dull and lacking humour
I is the symbol for electric current
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An up-to-date piece appears in a dull periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' seems to mean topical; it is the physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A diary is a daily personal record, a kind of journal.
